decks.title: Endocrine System — Part 1: Glands, the pancreas and the thyroid
goals: Distinguish endocrine from exocrine glands and locate the pituitary, thyroid, adrenals and pancreas
Explain how insulin and glucagon keep blood sugar steady
Relate too little or too much insulin or thyroxine to their disorders

slides.heading: The Endocrine System
slides.body_md: Part 1 — chemical messengers, the glands that make them, and how the pancreas and thyroid control the body.

visual.alt: Flow: an endocrine gland releases a hormone into the blood, which carries it to a target organ that responds

slides.narration: Your nerves send fast electrical messages. But your body also has a slower postal service. Glands release chemical messengers called hormones into the blood, and the blood delivers them to organs far away. In this part we meet the glands and two important hormone systems.

slides.heading: Endocrine and exocrine glands
slides.body_md: **Endocrine glands** are **ductless**: they pour **hormones** straight into the blood. **Exocrine glands** send their secretions through **ducts**.

visual.alt: Table comparing endocrine and exocrine glands on ducts, secretion, destination and examples

slides.narration: An exocrine gland is like a tap with a pipe. Saliva and sweat flow through ducts to where they are needed. An endocrine gland has no pipe. Its hormone soaks into the blood running through it and is carried all over the body.

slides.heading: Where the glands are
slides.body_md: **Pituitary**: pea-sized, at the base of the brain. **Thyroid**: two lobes in the neck. **Pancreas**: long and leaf-like, behind the stomach. **Adrenals**: a cap on each kidney.

slides.narration: Start at the head. The pea sized pituitary hangs below the brain. In the neck, the thyroid wraps its two lobes around the windpipe. Lower down, the long pancreas lies behind the stomach, and each kidney wears an adrenal gland like a cap.

slides.heading: The pancreas: a mixed gland
slides.body_md: The **acini** send pancreatic juice through a **duct** (exocrine). The **islets of Langerhans** release hormones into the **blood** (endocrine): **beta cells** make **insulin**, **alpha cells** make **glucagon**.

slides.narration: Most of the pancreas makes digestive juice, which flows through a duct to the duodenum. Scattered among these cells are tiny islands, the islets of Langerhans. Their beta cells make insulin and their alpha cells make glucagon, and both hormones go straight into the blood.

slides.narration: Think of the gland that sits in the loop of the duodenum.

slides.heading: Insulin and glucagon keep sugar steady
slides.body_md: **Insulin** lowers blood sugar; **glucagon** raises it. Together they hold it near **80–120 mg per 100 mL** of blood.

nodes.label: Blood sugar rises after a meal
Cells take up glucose; liver stores glycogen

visual.alt: Flow: a rise in blood sugar leads to insulin and storage as glycogen; a fall leads to glucagon and release of glucose; both return the level to normal

slides.narration: After a meal, sugar floods into the blood. The beta cells answer with insulin, and the liver stores the extra as glycogen. Between meals the level drops, so the alpha cells release glucagon and the liver turns glycogen back into glucose. The two hormones pull in opposite directions.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a sugar test
slides.body_md: Ravi and Meena drank glucose water after an overnight fast.
bullets: Step 1: Ravi rose by 145 − 90 = **55** in one hour, then fell by **40**: insulin is working.
Step 2: Meena started at **170**, above normal even when fasting, and rose by **120**.
Step 3: after two hours Meena is still **155** above Ravi: too little insulin, so **diabetes mellitus**.

slides.heading: Too little or too much insulin

rows: High blood sugar, sugar in urine, frequent urination, thirst, weight loss
Low blood sugar, shaking, sweating, fainting

visual.alt: Table of insulin disorders: diabetes mellitus from too little insulin, hypoglycaemia from too much

slides.narration: Too little insulin lets sugar build up in the blood until it spills into the urine and drags water with it. Too much insulin does the opposite. Blood sugar crashes, the brain is starved of fuel, and the person may faint.

slides.heading: The thyroid and thyroxine
slides.body_md: **Thyroxine** contains **iodine**. It controls the **basal metabolic rate** and is needed for normal **growth and mental development**.

rows: Stunted growth, delayed mental development, puffy face
Low metabolic rate, puffy skin, sluggishness
Swelling of the thyroid in the neck
Bulging eyes, fast heartbeat, weight loss, nervousness

visual.alt: Table of thyroid disorders with cause and main signs

slides.narration: Thyroxine sets the pace at which your cells burn food. Too little in a child slows growth and learning. Too little in an adult makes the person slow and puffy. Too much speeds everything up. And a lack of iodine makes the gland swell.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: naming the disorder
slides.body_md: Match the signs to the gland and the disorder.
bullets: Step 1: ask **which gland** controls the sign (sugar: pancreas; metabolism and growth: thyroid).
Step 2: ask **too much or too little**?
Step 3: ask **child or adult**, then name the disorder.

headers: Gland, too much or too little
rows: Child with stunted growth and slow learning

visual.alt: Worked table linking three sets of signs to the gland and the disorder

slides.narration: Three questions crack most of these problems. Which gland controls the sign? Is there too much hormone or too little? And is the patient a child or an adult? Answer them in order and the disorder names itself.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Endocrine glands are ductless and release hormones into the blood.
Pituitary at the base of the brain; thyroid in the neck; pancreas behind the stomach; adrenal on each kidney.
Insulin (beta cells) lowers blood sugar; glucagon (alpha cells) raises it.
Thyroxine controls metabolic rate, growth and mental development.

visual.alt: Summary table of disorders from too little or too much insulin and thyroxine

slides.narration: To recap. Hormones travel in the blood from ductless glands. Insulin and glucagon balance blood sugar. Thyroxine sets the pace of the body, and too little or too much of either hormone causes disease.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **beta cells → insulin**, **alpha cells → glucagon**; do not swap them.
For a disorder, give the **hormone**, **too much or too little**, and **child or adult**.
Diabetes **mellitus** is about **insulin**; do not confuse it with diabetes insipidus.
Draw glands in their **correct positions** on a body outline.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Keep alpha and beta cells straight. When you name a disorder, say which hormone, whether it is too much or too little, and at what age. And never mix up diabetes mellitus with diabetes insipidus.

goals: Describe the emergency effects of adrenaline and the role of the cortical hormones

slides.heading: Adrenal, Pituitary and Feedback
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the emergency gland, the master gland, and how hormones keep themselves in check.

visual.alt: Flow: the pituitary sends TSH to the thyroid, ACTH to the adrenal cortex, and FSH and LH to the gonads

slides.narration: One small gland under the brain sends orders to several others. In this part we meet that master gland, the adrenal gland that prepares you for emergencies, and the clever loop that stops a hormone from being over produced.

slides.heading: The adrenal gland
slides.body_md: Each adrenal gland has an outer **cortex** and an inner **medulla**.

rows: Salt and water balance; carbohydrate metabolism; some sex hormones
Prepares the body for an emergency

visual.alt: Table of the two regions of the adrenal gland, their hormones and main roles

slides.narration: The adrenal gland is really two glands in one. The outer cortex makes cortical hormones that keep salts, water and sugar in balance every day. The inner medulla makes adrenaline, which is saved for emergencies.

slides.heading: Adrenaline: fight or flight

rows: Less blood to the gut and skin

visual.alt: Table of five effects of adrenaline and how each helps in an emergency

slides.narration: Imagine a sudden loud crash. Within seconds your heart pounds, you breathe faster, your pupils widen and your blood fills with sugar. Every change gets the muscles ready to face the danger or to run from it. That is why adrenaline is called the emergency hormone.

slides.heading: Quick check: emergency sugar
slides.body_md: How does adrenaline give the muscles more glucose?
slides.narration: Where is glycogen stored?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a fright in numbers
slides.body_md: Arun's heart rate jumped from **72** to **117** beats per minute when a dog chased him.
bullets: Step 1: rise = 117 − 72 = **45** beats per minute.
Step 2: the hormone is **adrenaline** from the **adrenal medulla**.
Step 3: link the change to its use: more blood, oxygen and glucose to the leg muscles.

visual.alt: Worked table: heart rate 72 at rest, 117 during the chase, a rise of 45

slides.narration: Subtract to find the rise, then explain it. Adrenaline made Arun’s heart beat much faster, so more oxygen and sugar reached his leg muscles and he could pedal away. Once the danger passed, his heart rate slowly came back to normal.

slides.heading: The pituitary: master gland
slides.body_md: The **anterior lobe** makes **growth hormone** and the **tropic hormones** (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH). The **posterior lobe** releases **ADH** and **oxytocin**.

slides.narration: The pituitary sits just under the brain. Its front lobe makes growth hormone and tropic hormones, which switch on the thyroid, the adrenal cortex and the gonads. That control over other glands is why it is called the master gland. Its back lobe releases ADH and oxytocin.

slides.heading: Pituitary hormones and their work

rows: Makes the adrenal cortex release its hormones
Act on the testes and ovaries
More water reabsorbed in the kidney tubules
Contracts the uterus at childbirth; releases milk

visual.alt: Table of six pituitary hormones, their lobe and their action

slides.narration: Learn the hormones lobe by lobe. The anterior lobe gives growth hormone and four tropic hormones. The posterior lobe gives just two: ADH, which saves water in the kidneys, and oxytocin, which acts on the uterus and breasts.

slides.heading: When pituitary hormones go wrong

rows: Gigantism in children; acromegaly in adults
Diabetes insipidus: much dilute urine, thirst

visual.alt: Table of the effects of too little and too much growth hormone and ADH

slides.narration: Too little growth hormone in a child gives a short but well proportioned body. Too much gives a giant. In an adult the long bones cannot lengthen, so excess hormone enlarges the jaw, hands and feet instead. Too little ADH means large amounts of watery urine.

slides.heading: Quick check: childbirth
slides.body_md: Which hormone contracts the uterus during childbirth?
slides.narration: It comes from the posterior lobe.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: why so much urine?
slides.body_md: Mr Sen passes about **9** litres of urine a day; a typical adult passes about **1.5** litres.
bullets: Step 1: 9 ÷ 1.5 = **6** times the usual volume.
Step 2: blood sugar normal and no sugar in urine, so **not** diabetes mellitus.
Step 3: dilute urine means water is not reabsorbed: shortage of **ADH**, called **diabetes insipidus**.

headers: What it rules in or out

slides.narration: Use the clues one at a time. Mr Sen passes about 6 times the usual urine. There is no sugar, so insulin is not the problem. The urine is watery, so his kidneys are not taking water back. The missing hormone is ADH.

slides.body_md: **Low thyroxine → more TSH → thyroid makes more thyroxine. High thyroxine → less TSH.** This is **negative feedback**.

slides.narration: Feedback also explains goitre. Without iodine the thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine. The pituitary keeps sending more and more TSH, and the thyroid, pushed to work harder and harder, grows into a swelling in the neck.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Adrenal cortex: cortical hormones for salts, water and sugar; medulla: adrenaline for emergencies.
Pituitary is the master gland: tropic hormones control other glands.
Growth hormone: dwarfism, gigantism, acromegaly. ADH: diabetes insipidus.
Thyroxine controls TSH release by negative feedback.

visual.alt: Summary table of three glands, their key hormones and a key word

slides.narration: To recap. Adrenaline prepares you for danger. The pituitary directs the other glands and controls growth and water balance. And negative feedback between thyroxine and TSH keeps the thyroid working at just the right pace.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: **Dwarf vs cretin:** a pituitary dwarf has **normal intelligence**; a cretin does not.
**Gigantism** is in children, **acromegaly** in adults.
In a feedback answer, say what happens when thyroxine is **high** and when it is **low**.
ADH acts on the **kidney tubules**; oxytocin on the **uterus**.

notes.title: Endocrine System — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Endocrine and exocrine glands; where the glands are
sections.body_md:
**Hormones** are chemical messengers secreted by **endocrine glands** directly into the **blood**, which carries them to **target organs**. They act slowly compared with nerves, but their effects last longer.

| Endocrine (ductless) glands | Exocrine glands |
|---|---|
| No ducts | Have ducts |
| Secrete hormones into the blood | Secrete enzymes, sweat, tears, saliva onto a surface or into a cavity |
| Thyroid, pituitary, adrenal | Salivary, sweat, lacrimal glands |

The **pancreas** is a **heterocrine (mixed)** gland: its acini are exocrine (pancreatic juice through a duct) and its **islets of Langerhans** are endocrine.

**Location and shape**
- **Pituitary:** pea-sized, at the **base of the brain**, attached to the hypothalamus; anterior and posterior lobes.
- **Thyroid:** two lobes joined by an isthmus (butterfly or H-shaped), in the **neck** on either side of the windpipe below the larynx.
- **Pancreas:** long, leaf-like, lying **behind the stomach** with its head in the loop of the duodenum.
- **Adrenal:** a cap (roughly triangular) on **top of each kidney**; outer cortex, inner medulla.

key_terms.definition_md: A chemical messenger secreted by a ductless gland and carried by blood to a target organ.
A ductless gland that releases hormones into the blood.
A gland with both exocrine and endocrine parts, such as the pancreas.

sections.heading: 2. Pancreas (insulin, glucagon) and thyroid (thyroxine)
sections.body_md:
**Islets of Langerhans:** **beta cells** secrete **insulin**; **alpha cells** secrete **glucagon**.
- **Insulin lowers blood sugar:** cells take up glucose; the liver and muscles store extra glucose as **glycogen**.
- **Glucagon raises blood sugar:** liver glycogen is changed into **glucose**.
- Together they keep blood sugar near **80–120 mg per 100 mL** of blood.

| Insulin | Effect |
|---|---|
| Hyposecretion | **Diabetes mellitus:** high blood sugar, glucose in urine (glycosuria), frequent urination, thirst, tiredness, weight loss |
| Hypersecretion (or overdose) | **Hypoglycaemia:** low blood sugar, shaking, sweating, fainting (insulin shock) |

**Thyroxine** (contains **iodine**) controls the **basal metabolic rate** and is needed for normal **physical and mental development**.

| Thyroxine | Effect |
|---|---|
| Too little in childhood | **Cretinism:** stunted, disproportionate growth, delayed mental development, puffy face |
| Too little in adults | **Myxoedema:** low metabolic rate, puffy skin, sluggishness, weight gain |
| Lack of iodine | **Simple goitre:** enlarged thyroid |
| Too much | **Exophthalmic goitre:** protruding eyes, high metabolic rate, fast heartbeat, weight loss, nervousness |

sections.heading: 4. Pituitary gland: the master gland
sections.body_md:
The pituitary is called the **master gland** because its **tropic hormones** control other endocrine glands.

| Lobe | Hormone | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior | **Growth hormone (GH)** | Growth of bones and muscles |
| Anterior | **TSH** | Stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine |
| Anterior | **ACTH** | Stimulates the adrenal cortex |
| Anterior | **FSH, LH** | Act on the gonads (testes, ovaries) |
| Posterior | **ADH (vasopressin)** | Increases reabsorption of water in the kidney tubules |
| Posterior | **Oxytocin** | Contracts the uterus at childbirth; milk release |

**Growth hormone:** too little in childhood → **dwarfism** (short but proportionate body, normal intelligence); too much in childhood → **gigantism**; too much in adults → **acromegaly** (enlarged jaw, hands and feet).

**ADH:** too little → **diabetes insipidus** (large volumes of dilute urine, thirst, no sugar in urine); too much → little, concentrated urine and water retention.

key_terms.definition_md: A hormone that stimulates another endocrine gland.
Antidiuretic hormone; increases water reabsorption in the kidneys.
Enlarged jaw, hands and feet due to excess growth hormone in adults.

sections.heading: 5. Feedback: TSH and thyroxine
sections.body_md:
The secretion of thyroxine is controlled by **negative feedback**:
- **Low thyroxine** in the blood → anterior pituitary releases **more TSH** → thyroid releases more thyroxine.
- **High thyroxine** → pituitary releases **less TSH** → thyroid releases less thyroxine.

So the level of the hormone itself controls the signal that releases it, keeping it **steady**.

**Simple goitre and feedback:** without iodine, thyroxine stays low, TSH stays high, and the overstimulated thyroid **enlarges**.

key_terms.definition_md: Control in which a rise in a hormone reduces the signal that causes its release.
Thyroid-stimulating hormone of the anterior pituitary.

questions.stem_md: Explain how insulin and glucagon together keep the blood sugar level within the normal range.

answer.model_answer_md: After a meal blood sugar rises, so the **beta cells** release **insulin**: cells take up glucose and the liver stores the extra as **glycogen**, and the level falls. When blood sugar falls, the **alpha cells** release **glucagon**: the liver changes **glycogen back to glucose**, and the level rises. The two act in opposite ways, keeping it near 80–120 mg per 100 mL.

questions.solution_md: Opposite actions of insulin and glucagon.

| 0 h | 90 | 170 |
| 1 h | 145 | 290 |

**(b)** 120 mg per 100 mL

2. An injection puts it **directly into the blood**, where it must act, in a measured dose.

questions.solution_md:

**(b)** Rise $= 290 - 170 = 120$ mg per 100 mL.

**(c)** Insulin released and acted.

**(d)** (i) Any two signs.

(ii) Protein digested; direct to blood.

**(e)** Hypoglycaemia; glucagon corrects it.
